title: Washing
hookLine: water over each hand, and a blessing, to begin clean
tomorrow: a line said morning and night. what does it ask you to do first?

cards: You went to bed after a fight. Nothing dramatic: a sharp tone about the dishes, a door shut a little too hard, both of you being very polite by bedtime. You wake up and it's all still there, waiting in the hallway.

So how do you start the day clean, when yesterday hasn't been put away? Jewish tradition starts every morning the same way, whether the night was peaceful or not. Before anything else, you wash your hands.

teach.h: A CUP, ONE HAND, THEN THE OTHER.
teach.b: It's called netilat yadayim, the washing of the hands. You fill a cup with water and pour it over one hand, then the other, in turn.
Then comes a blessing the Talmud lists among the morning blessings: blessed are You, who made us holy with commandments and commanded us about washing the hands.
Here's the surprise worth telling a friend: this washing isn't about germs. Your hands might already be clean. It's about beginning.
Some explain it by the priests, who washed hands and feet before they served in the sanctuary, as Exodus tells it. Every morning, you get the same treatment: ready to serve, starting fresh.
The Psalms ask who may go up to the mountain of the LORD, and answer: "He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart." Water does the hands. The heart takes longer.
So what does this give you the morning after a fight? Not a pretend reset. The fight happened.
But the water says the day doesn't have to be yesterday's day. You start with a small physical act, pouring, one hand, then the other, and a blessing that names the moment as holy.
Then you walk into the kitchen with clean hands, and you get to make the first move. Maybe it's an apology. Maybe it's making two coffees instead of one.
A clean start isn't forgetting. It's choosing how today begins.

how: In the morning, Jews traditionally wash with a cup, pouring water over each hand in turn, often keeping a cup and basin by the bed or in the bathroom, and say the blessing al netilat yadayim.

o: pouring water over each hand to begin the day
rinsing dishes after a meal, with a blessing
a bath taken before every holiday meal

p: pour over one hand, then the other
clean hands, and a pure heart

s: the morning hand-washing is mainly about hygiene
your hands may already be clean. it's about beginning, like the priests washing before they served.
the Talmud lists a blessing for washing the hands among the morning blessings
blessed are You… who commanded us about washing the hands.
a clean start means pretending yesterday never happened
the fight happened. the water says today can begin differently, and you make the first move.

games.q: your little brother broke your headphones yesterday and you yelled. this morning he's avoiding you at breakfast. what fits a clean start?
o: make the first small move: a word, or pouring his cereal too.
wait until he apologizes, since he broke them first.
act like nothing happened and never bring it up.
games.why: the washing doesn't erase yesterday; it begins today. clean hands, and then the first move is yours.

practice: Hold your hands out, palms up, as if a cup of water were about to pour: one hand, then the other, slowly, feeling each in turn. If you say blessings, say the one for washing the hands quietly; tomorrow morning it can be real water.
Then, hands still open, choose one first move you will make today toward someone you are at odds with.

wordCard.voice: Washing: netilat yadayim, water poured over each hand and a blessing, every morning. Not about dirt; about beginning.

orig.note: Hebrew: the washing of the hands, with a cup, and its blessing.

carryVoice: Your line: clean start. The water does the hands; you make the first move. See you tomorrow.
